_comment: AP Networking Topic 3.5, Firewalls and filtering. Sub-skills 2.B and 2.C.
WHY A FILE AND NOT A RULE BUILDER
EK 3.5.C.4 says the ORDER of a rule set decides which traffic is permitted.
A firewall rule set is a text file read top to bottom, so reading one in a
terminal is not a metaphor for the work, it is the work. The Rule Order
game teaches the same idea by letting a student rearrange rules; this lab
teaches the half that comes first in real life, which is finding the
shadowed rule in somebody else's list while a service is down.
Nothing in acl-current.txt is a wrong rule. Rule 20 is correct, rule 30 is
correct, and rule 20 sits above rule 30 and matches everything rule 30 was
written for. Diffing against last week's working copy is what makes it
visible, which is why check 6 exists and why check 7 is gated behind the
diagnosis rather than offered alongside it.
title: Finance cannot reach the reporting server
page_title: AP Networking Lab: Find the Shadowed Firewall Rule | Topic 3.5
seo_description: A service went down after a firewall change and every rule in the list is correct. Find the one that shadows another and fix the order. AP Networking Topic 3.5.
brief: Since Tuesday, nobody in finance can open the reporting server. Everything else works. The firewall was changed on Monday evening and the person who changed it is on leave.
You have the current rule set, last week's copy, the ticket, and the segment map.
1. Read the ticket before the rules. It tells you which traffic is supposed to work.
2. Find out which subnet finance actually is.
3. Read the rule set the way the firewall reads it: top to bottom, first match wins.
4. Compare it against last week, when this worked.
No rule in this list is wrong. That is the difficulty.

questions.prompt: Which rule stops finance reaching the reporting server?
options: Rule 30, because it permits the wrong port
Rule 20, because it matches finance traffic first and denies it
Rule 40, because a catch-all deny always blocks everything
Rule 10, because it permits the wrong subnet
questions.explain: EK 3.5.C.4. Rule 20 denies the whole 10.20.0.0/16 range to the server segment, and finance at 10.20.30.0/24 sits inside it. A firewall stops at the first rule that matches, so rule 30, which was written to permit exactly this traffic, is never reached. Rule 30 is not wrong. It is unreachable, and a rule set review that reads each rule on its own cannot tell the difference.

options: Change rule 30 to permit any source
questions.explain: Move the specific permit above the broad deny. Deleting rule 20 would also open the rest of 10.20.0.0/16 to the server segment, which is the isolation somebody deliberately added on Monday. Deleting the catch-all deny would open the firewall generally. Widening rule 30 to any source gives every subnet the access only finance was meant to have. Specific rules go above general ones, and the general rule keeps doing its job underneath.

questions.prompt: After the change, which pair of results together proves it?
options: Finance reaches the reporting server, and the change was saved
Finance reaches the reporting server, and a host elsewhere in 10.20.0.0/16 still cannot
The firewall log shows rule 30 matching
No error appears in the firewall console
questions.explain: One thing that must now work and one that must still fail. Testing only that finance got in would also pass if you had deleted rule 20 and opened the whole range, which is the failure you were trying to avoid. A control that both permits and blocks needs a test for each half.

checks.label: Read the ticket before touching the rules
Find out which subnet finance actually is
Read the rule set that is applied now
Search the rules for the finance subnet rather than skimming
Name the rule that shadows the one written for finance
Compare against last week, when it worked
Choose the fix that keeps Monday's isolation
VERIFY: pick the pair of results that proves it
